items.title: The angles of a triangle on a globe don't add to 180 degrees
items.claim: Draw a triangle from the North Pole to the equator at 0 degrees longitude, along the equator to 90 degrees longitude, and back to the North Pole. All three angles are 90 degrees. Total: 270.
items.prompt: How can a triangle have 270 degrees?

options.text: On a curved surface, the angle sum exceeds 180 by an amount proportional to the area enclosed (spherical excess); on a sphere of radius R, sum = 180 + (area / R^2) in radians times 180/pi

items.reveal:
On a flat Euclidean plane, the angles of a triangle sum to exactly 180 degrees.

On a sphere (positive curvature), the sum is more than 180. The excess is proportional to the area: Sum - 180 = (Area / R^2) * (180/pi) for a sphere of radius R. The example triangle (pole-equator-equator-pole) covers 1/8 of the Earth's surface — area ~ 6.4 * 10^7 square km — and has excess 90 degrees.

On a hyperbolic plane (negative curvature), the sum is LESS than 180. The deficit is proportional to area.

This is the deepest test of non-Euclidean geometry: by measuring the angle sum of a triangle, you can tell what kind of space you're in.

Gauss attempted to measure the angle sum of a triangle formed by three mountain peaks (Hohenhagen, Brocken, Inselsberg) in 1820s to test whether space itself is Euclidean. He found no measurable deviation from 180, given his instruments' precision.

General relativity: mass curves space-time. Light follows geodesics through curved space-time. Two photons from a distant source, passing on either side of the Sun, converge (negative curvature in tested region's measurement frame). Detected during the 1919 solar eclipse — confirmation of Einstein.
items.why: Triangles seem to obviously sum to 180. They do on flat surfaces. Real Earth navigation, general relativity, and modern cosmology all use non-Euclidean geometry where triangle sums are observably different.

items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.

items.title: Matrices don't commute — and that's why quantum mechanics works
items.claim: AB is not generally equal to BA for matrices. The order of operations matters. This isn't a defect — it's the most important feature of matrix algebra and the mathematical foundation of quantum uncertainty.

options.text: Matrices represent linear transformations of vectors; applying transformation A then B is generally not the same as B then A. The non-commutativity reflects that composition of transformations in higher dimensions does NOT commute in general
AB = BA always works for invertible matrices

items.reveal:
For matrices, AB and BA are generally different — and AB is well-defined only when A's columns equal B's rows. Even for square matrices of the same size, AB and BA can differ wildly.

Example: A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].
AB = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].
BA = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]. Different.

When does AB = BA? Some special cases: scalar multiples of identity; same diagonal matrix; simultaneously diagonalisable matrices; powers of the same matrix.

The commutator [A, B] = AB - BA measures the non-commutativity. For ordinary numbers it's always zero; for matrices it can be anything.

In QUANTUM MECHANICS:
- Physical observables are represented as matrices (or operators on Hilbert space).
- The commutator of position and momentum: [x, p] = i * hbar. Non-zero!
- Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: the variance of two non-commuting observables, in any state, has a lower bound proportional to the commutator. You can't simultaneously know position and momentum precisely.

This is not a measurement limitation — it's a structural feature of the math. Eigenvectors of non-commuting matrices are different; states have to choose between definite x and definite p.

Lie groups and algebras: continuous symmetry transformations form groups whose generators are matrices with commutation relations. The group SU(3) underlies the strong nuclear force; SU(2) describes weak force and quantum spin; U(1) describes electromagnetism. The standard model of particle physics is built from non-commuting matrices.

In computer graphics: rotation matrices in 3D don't commute (mentioned in another card). The order matters when composing transformations.
items.why: Multiplication seems naturally commutative. For matrices it isn't — and the depth of this fact is that quantum mechanics, particle physics, computer graphics, and most of modern physics rely on it.
